chapters.1: Matthew traces Jesus' family line back through David to Abraham, establishing his legal right to be Israel's promised king. It then describes how Mary, engaged to Joseph, became pregnant through the Holy Spirit, and an angel reassures Joseph in a dream that the child, to be named Jesus, will save his people from their sins.
chapters.2: Wise men from the east follow a star to find the newborn Jesus and bring him gifts, while King Herod, threatened by reports of a new king, orders the massacre of young boys in Bethlehem. Joseph is warned in dreams to flee with Mary and Jesus to Egypt and later to settle safely in Nazareth once Herod has died.
chapters.3: John the Baptist appears in the wilderness calling people to repent and be baptized in preparation for the coming kingdom of heaven. Jesus comes to be baptized by John, and as he does, the Holy Spirit descends on him like a dove and God's voice declares him his beloved Son.
chapters.4: Jesus is tempted by the devil in the wilderness with offers of food, power, and safety, but resists each temptation using Scripture. He then begins his public ministry in Galilee, calling his first disciples, including fishermen Peter, Andrew, James, and John, and healing many people of sickness and disease.
chapters.5: Jesus begins the Sermon on the Mount with the Beatitudes, blessing qualities like humility, mercy, and peacemaking, and calls his followers to be "salt" and "light" in the world. He then deepens the meaning of Old Testament commands about anger, lust, oaths, and revenge, teaching a higher standard of love that even extends to enemies.
chapters.6: Jesus teaches that genuine acts of giving, prayer, and fasting should be done quietly for God rather than for public praise, and gives his followers the model prayer now known as the Lord's Prayer. He also warns against storing up earthly wealth and worrying about daily needs, urging his listeners to trust God and seek his kingdom first.
chapters.7: Jesus warns against judging others hypocritically and instructs his followers to ask God confidently for what they need, trusting his fatherly generosity. He summarizes right living in the Golden Rule, warns of false prophets and empty religious talk, and closes by comparing those who act on his words to a wise builder whose house survives the storm.
chapters.8: Jesus heals a man with leprosy, a Roman centurion's servant from a distance after being impressed by the officer's faith, and Peter's mother-in-law, along with many others. He then calms a violent storm at sea with a word and drives demons out of two men into a herd of pigs, showing his authority over sickness, nature, and evil spirits.
chapters.9: Jesus forgives and heals a paralyzed man, then calls the tax collector Matthew to follow him and eats with other social outcasts, explaining that he came for sinners, not the self-righteous. He also heals a woman who touches his robe in faith, raises a ruler's daughter from death, and restores sight and speech to the blind and mute, while noting the growing opposition from religious leaders.
chapters.10: Jesus sends out his twelve disciples with authority to heal and cast out demons, instructing them to travel simply and rely on others' hospitality as they preach that the kingdom of heaven is near. He warns them that following him will bring persecution and even family conflict, but reassures them that God values them deeply and will not forget their faithfulness.
chapters.11: Jesus answers John the Baptist's disciples, who ask if he truly is the promised one, by pointing to his miracles as evidence, then praises John as the greatest of the prophets even though people rejected his message. He criticizes the unrepentant towns where he worked miracles, and ends with a gentle invitation for the weary to come to him and find rest.
chapters.12: Religious leaders criticize Jesus and his disciples for breaking sabbath customs, but he insists that mercy and human need take priority over rigid rule-keeping. After healing a man's hand on the sabbath, he is accused of working by Satan's power when he casts out a demon, which he refutes logically, and he warns that rejecting the Holy Spirit's work is a serious, unforgivable sin.
chapters.13: Jesus teaches a series of parables about the kingdom of heaven, including the parable of the sower, explaining why different people respond differently to his message, and the parable of the wheat and weeds, showing good and evil coexisting until final judgment. Further short parables compare the kingdom to a mustard seed, yeast, hidden treasure, and a valuable pearl, emphasizing its hidden but surpassing worth.
chapters.14: King Herod has John the Baptist beheaded to satisfy a rash promise made during a feast, and when Jesus hears the news he withdraws, though crowds follow him and he miraculously feeds five thousand people with five loaves and two fish. That night Jesus walks on water to reach his disciples' boat, and when Peter tries to walk toward him he begins to sink from doubt before Jesus rescues him.
chapters.15: Jesus confronts religious leaders for valuing human traditions over genuine obedience to God, teaching that true impurity comes from the heart, not from ritual uncleanness like unwashed hands. He commends the persistent faith of a Gentile woman by healing her daughter, and feeds another large crowd of four thousand people using seven loaves and a few fish.
chapters.16: Jesus warns his disciples to be wary of the corrupting influence of the Pharisees and Sadducees, then asks who they believe he is; Peter declares him the Christ, the Son of the living God, and Jesus says he will build his church on this confession. Jesus then begins telling his disciples plainly that he must suffer, die, and rise again, and teaches that true followers must be willing to give up their own lives for his sake.
chapters.17: Jesus is transfigured on a mountain before Peter, James, and John, appearing radiant alongside Moses and Elijah while God's voice affirms him as his Son. Coming down, Jesus heals a boy his disciples could not help because of their lack of faith, again predicts his coming death and resurrection, and miraculously provides payment for the temple tax from a fish's mouth.
chapters.18: Jesus teaches that greatness in his kingdom means becoming humble like a child, and warns strongly against causing others, especially the vulnerable, to stumble in faith. He gives guidance for addressing conflict between believers and tells the parable of the unforgiving servant to show that genuine forgiveness, not just a count of offenses, is required of his followers.
chapters.19: Jesus teaches that marriage is a lifelong union intended by God, allowing divorce only in cases of unfaithfulness, and blesses children brought to him despite the disciples' objections. When a wealthy young man cannot bring himself to give up his riches to follow Jesus, Jesus explains how hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of heaven, though nothing is impossible for God.
chapters.20: Jesus tells the parable of workers in a vineyard who are all paid the same regardless of how many hours they worked, illustrating God's generous grace rather than strict fairness by human standards. He again predicts his death and resurrection, corrects James and John's mother for seeking special status for her sons, and heals two blind men near Jericho.
chapters.21: Jesus enters Jerusalem riding a donkey to the crowd's shouts of praise, then drives the merchants and money changers out of the temple, declaring it a house of prayer. He curses a fruitless fig tree as an object lesson, and when questioned about his authority, tells parables about two sons and a vineyard's tenants that expose the religious leaders' rejection of God's messengers, including himself.
chapters.22: Jesus tells the parable of a king's wedding feast whose invited guests refuse to come, showing how God's invitation extends beyond those who first reject it. Religious leaders then try to trap him with questions about paying taxes to Caesar, the resurrection, and the greatest commandment, and Jesus answers each skillfully, also stumping them by asking how the Christ can be both David's son and David's Lord.
chapters.23: Jesus strongly criticizes the scribes and Pharisees for their hypocrisy, performing religious duties for show while neglecting genuine justice, mercy, and faith. He pronounces a series of "woes" against their empty legalism and spiritual blindness, and mourns over Jerusalem's repeated rejection of God's messengers.
chapters.24: Jesus predicts the destruction of the Jerusalem temple and, when asked about the end of the age, describes wars, famines, persecution, and false prophets as signs preceding his return. He urges watchfulness since no one but the Father knows the exact timing, comparing it to the suddenness of the flood in Noah's day, and calls his followers to remain faithful and ready.
chapters.25: Jesus tells the parable of the ten bridesmaids, warning that his followers must be prepared for his return at an unknown hour, and the parable of the talents, teaching that his followers are responsible for faithfully using what they've been given. He then describes a final judgment where people are separated like sheep from goats based on how they treated those in need, since caring for the needy means caring for him.
chapters.26: A woman anoints Jesus with expensive perfume in preparation for his burial, while Judas Iscariot secretly agrees to betray him for thirty pieces of silver. At the Last Supper Jesus institutes what becomes known as communion, predicts Peter's denial, and is arrested in Gethsemane after praying in anguish, then faces an unjust nighttime trial before the high priest while Peter denies knowing him three times.
chapters.27: Jesus is handed over to the Roman governor Pilate, who reluctantly has him crucified after the crowd demands it over the release of a prisoner named Barabbas; Judas, overcome with guilt, hangs himself. Jesus dies on the cross after hours of mockery and suffering, dramatic signs accompany his death, and his body is placed in a tomb sealed and guarded at the religious leaders' request.
chapters.28: Women find Jesus' tomb empty, and an angel tells them he has risen from the dead, a message Jesus himself soon confirms by appearing to them. The book closes with Jesus commissioning his eleven remaining disciples to make disciples of all nations, baptizing and teaching them, and promising to be with them always.
